title: Sync-over-async deadlocks (.Result, .Wait) and thread-pool starvation
hook: Calling .Result or .Wait() on a Task blocks the current thread until the Task finishes. On a UI thread or thread-pool under load, that is how deadlocks and starvation happen — even in ASP.NET Core.

blocks.text: Sync-over-async means blocking a thread waiting for an async operation to complete — typically via task.Result, task.Wait(), or task.GetAwaiter().GetResult(). The async method's continuation may need the blocked thread (SynchronizationContext deadlock) or a free pool thread (starvation). ASP.NET Core has no request SynchronizationContext, so the classic UI deadlock does not apply — but blocking still holds a pool thread for the entire I/O wait, which under concurrent load exhausts the pool before the CPU is saturated.

entries.plainDefinition: Blocking a thread to wait for an async operation instead of awaiting it.
entries.example: var data = GetDataAsync().Result; // blocks caller thread

entries.plainDefinition: All pool threads are blocked waiting; new work queues up with idle CPUs.
entries.example: 100 concurrent requests each calling .Result on HTTP — pool exhausted.

entries.plainDefinition: Blocking wait that unwraps AggregateException like .Result but works on void-returning async.
Blocked thread is the only thread the continuation can run on.
entries.example: UI thread blocked in .Result; continuation needs UI thread.

blocks.text: A library method that calls .Result internally works in a unit test but deadlocks in WinForms or classic ASP.NET. In ASP.NET Core, the same pattern does not deadlock but caps throughput: each blocked request holds a Kestrel thread-pool thread for the full Redis or HTTP latency. At 200 concurrent requests with 50 ms I/O, you need 200 blocked threads — the pool grows slowly (hill-climbing) and requests queue with processors idle. Production incidents from sync-over-async show up as rising queue depth in dotnet-counters, not as a hung UI.

blocks.title: The fix is always async all the way
blocks.body: Make the caller async and await. If you truly cannot (legacy Main, COM interop), use GetAwaiter().GetResult() only at the top-level entry point — never deep in a library called from many contexts.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: SynchronizationContext deadlock
items.body: UI or legacy ASP.NET thread calls .Result. Async continuation tries to post back to that thread. Thread is blocked. Deadlock.

items.title: Thread-pool starvation
items.body: Many pool threads block in .Wait() on I/O. Pool cannot grow fast enough. New work queues. Latency spikes.

items.title: Hill-climbing delay
items.body: .NET thread pool injects threads slowly. A burst of blocking calls creates a window where everything waits.

items.title: Fix
items.body: async/await all the way. Libraries use ConfigureAwait(false). Never .Result in shared code.

snippet.label: Classic UI deadlock — stack trace pattern
snippet.explanation: The UI thread is inside Wait/Result. The continuation is queued to SynchronizationContext.Send on the same thread. Neither can proceed — classic deadlock stack.

snippet.label: ASP.NET Core starvation — no deadlock, still broken
snippet.explanation: No SynchronizationContext means no classic deadlock. But each .Result holds a thread for the full wait — scalability collapses under load.

snippet.label: Library anti-pattern that poisons callers
snippet.explanation: Libraries that block internally force every caller into sync-over-async. Top-level Main is the only acceptable GetResult site.

snippet.label: Diagnose starvation with dotnet-counters
snippet.explanation: How to prove it in production: rising ThreadPool QueueLength with low CPU is the signature of sync-over-async or blocking I/O on pool threads.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Claiming ASP.NET Core is 'safe' for .Result because there is no deadlock — starvation is still catastrophic. Using .Result in a library because 'the caller is async anyway.' Wrapping blocking I/O in Task.Run and then calling .Result — still wastes a thread. Assuming Task.Wait with a timeout avoids deadlock — the continuation may still never run on a captured context.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: capture a stack trace during an incident — blocked threads show System.Threading.Tasks.Task.InternalWait or Task.GetResultCore. Pair with dotnet-counters ThreadPool QueueLength and ThreadPool ThreadCount. Under a load test, sync-over-async produces climbing thread count with flat CPU. The fix is never 'increase MinThreads' as the first response — that masks the problem. Async all the way, or isolate blocking to a dedicated thread (BackgroundService with a blocking consumer) with explicit capacity limits.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: await on UI; ConfigureAwait(false) in library
Core API slow under load, low CPU
Occasional hang in test, fine locally
Remove blocking; do not just raise MinThreads

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying 'ASP.NET Core has no SynchronizationContext so .Result is fine.' It is not — you starve the pool. Saying 'I use .Result for simplicity' without acknowledging scalability cost. Recommending ThreadPool.SetMinThreads as the primary fix instead of removing sync-over-async. Not being able to read a deadlock stack trace showing SynchronizationContext.Send blocked inside Task.Wait.

interviewTakeaways: Sync-over-async blocks a thread for the full async wait — .Result, .Wait(), and GetAwaiter().GetResult().
Classic deadlock needs SynchronizationContext; ASP.NET Core gets starvation instead — still catastrophic under load.
In production, watch dotnet-counters ThreadPool QueueLength spike with low CPU — the signature of sync-over-async.

60s: Never .Result in libraries. UI deadlock is context capture plus blocked thread. Core starves the pool without deadlocking. Fix: async all the way. Prove with dotnet-counters and stack traces showing Task.Wait.
Follow-up: when is GetAwaiter().GetResult() acceptable — only at process entry points like Main?
commonPitfalls: Saying '.Result is fine in ASP.NET Core' gets you rejected — pool starvation caps throughput with idle CPUs.
Using .Result in a shared library because tests pass — production WinForms or high-concurrency Core will fail differently.
Strong answer: 'I async all the way. .Result causes context deadlock on UI or pool starvation in Core. I diagnose with ThreadPool QueueLength in dotnet-counters.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: JS has no .Result — but sync fs.readFileSync or a tight while loop inside async code blocks the single thread for everyone. C# sync-over-async blocks one pool thread per call; the damage scales with concurrency, not a single loop.

TypeScript/JavaScript forces you to await or use .then — there is no GetResult(). C#'s .Result is a footgun that TS avoids by design. The C# equivalent of blocking the event loop is blocking every pool thread.
